Pregnancy

Planks during pregnancy: adapting core exercise and returning after birth

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A plank is one way to challenge the muscles that support your trunk. It is optional, and the version that suited you before pregnancy may become uncomfortable. The useful question is whether a particular exercise fits your pregnancy, symptoms and control: not whether every pregnant person should keep or stop all planks.

Start with your pregnancy and your usual activity

Appropriate strength work can be part of activity in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Discuss your routine with your maternity team, especially if you are new to exercise, have a medical condition or develop a pregnancy complication. A previous comfortable plank is not permanent clearance when circumstances change.

A plank holds the trunk against gravity while the arms and feet or knees provide support. Different versions create different demands. You do not need a full floor plank to stay active, and pregnancy is not the time to chase your longest hold. A qualified pregnancy-exercise professional or pelvic-health physiotherapist can help you choose an appropriate version.

Benefits belong to a balanced programme

Suitable activity can support fitness, mood, strength and back comfort. Core training can help you practise controlling the trunk during everyday movement. These are potential benefits of appropriate activity, not promises that a plank will prevent pain, make labour easy or speed every recovery.

Planks do not replace individual pelvic-floor care. Leaking, urgency, pelvic heaviness or pain deserve assessment; stronger bracing is not always the answer. A useful routine allows normal breathing and includes movement you enjoy, such as walking or swimming where suitable, rather than treating one abdominal exercise as essential.

Understand separation without blaming yourself

As pregnancy grows, the tissue between the two main columns of abdominal muscle stretches and becomes wider. Persistent widening is often called diastasis recti. The amount varies, and a changed abdominal shape does not mean you caused an injury or failed to exercise correctly.

Studies of selected abdominal exercise programmes during pregnancy have not supported a blanket claim that abdominal exercise necessarily worsens the gap. They also do not prove that every plank is safe for everyone or that one exercise prevents separation. The 2024 and 2025 trials assessed particular programmes and measured the gap; neither is a universal plank prescription.

Use doming and symptoms to adjust the load

A ridge or dome along the midline during effort is a reason to review the movement, not proof by itself that tissue has torn. If doming is pronounced or you lose control, reduce the difficulty, shorten the effort or choose another movement. Ask a physiotherapist if the change persists or you are unsure what you are seeing.

Stop a movement that causes pain, pelvic pressure or leaking, and arrange assessment rather than repeatedly pushing through it. Difficulty breathing normally, a sagging back or excessive neck gripping also suggests the exercise is too demanding at that moment. Do not force the abdomen inward or try to hold a hard brace all day.

Try a supported incline if it suits you

An incline moves the upper-body support above the floor. A gentle wall version uses the hands around shoulder height against a solid wall, with the feet a short distance back and the body comfortably aligned. A higher support and smaller lean can make the task easier. A clinician or trained instructor can check the setup and whether it is appropriate for you.

If using a fixed counter, it must securely support your weight and leave room for the bump; avoid wheeled chairs, loose furniture or slippery surfaces. Keep breathing, avoid letting the lower back sag and come out before control deteriorates. A wall or counter variation is an option, not a guarantee against symptoms or separation. You can stop planks and choose another exercise.

Knee-supported versions are another option

For someone who can get down to and up from the floor comfortably, keeping the knees supported reduces the lever compared with a full toes-supported plank. Your helper may suggest forearm or hand support, a shorter effort, or remaining on hands and knees instead. Keep room for the abdomen and avoid forcing an unfamiliar position.

Lowering the knees does not automatically make every exercise suitable. If pain, pressure, marked doming or breath-holding continues, choose an easier alternative and seek advice. Pregnancy guidance also describes options such as a supported wall pushup, controlled hands-and-knees movements or a modified side plank; none is compulsory and each still needs an appropriate level of support.

Adapt as pregnancy changes

Fatigue may make a familiar exercise less appealing early on; later, the bump, balance and joint comfort may alter what works. There is no single week when everyone must stop planks or a fixed hold time everyone must reach. Reduce the load or switch activities as needed, without using discomfort as a challenge to overcome.

Keep cool, drink regularly and avoid strenuous exercise when unwell. Do not lie on the bump or force compressed, painful twisting positions. Later in pregnancy, avoid prolonged flat-on-back exercise and change position if dizzy or uncomfortable. Crunches and twists are not one uniform category, so ask about the actual movement rather than assuming all are safe or all inevitably cause diastasis.

Know when changing the exercise is not enough

Stop and contact your maternity team promptly for bleeding, fluid leakage, persistent abdominal pain or regular painful contractions. A reduction in your baby's usual movements needs immediate maternity advice. Do not finish the set or wait to see whether a different plank fixes these symptoms.

Seek immediate medical help for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe persistent abdominal pain, a severe headache or visual change, or a newly painful swollen leg. Tell the team that you are pregnant or have recently given birth. These symptoms need assessment, not a home exercise adjustment.

Return gradually after birth

A comfortable pregnancy routine does not establish what is appropriate immediately after delivery. Following an uncomplicated birth, gentle movement may begin when you feel ready; a caesarean, significant tears or other complications need individual advice before strenuous work. Early recovery usually starts with easier movement and coordinated breathing, not demanding planks or sit-ups.

Progression can move from gentle supported work toward more challenging positions when healing, symptoms and control allow. Postnatal physiotherapy guidance uses wall and knee-supported stages before full planks for selected people. That is a possible rehabilitation sequence, not a mandatory timetable. Stop or step back if pain, pressure, leaking or marked doming increases.

A finger-width gap is not a clearance test

The space between the muscles is only one part of assessment. Do not decide that a full plank is safe because fewer than one or two fingers fit, or that all movement must stop until the gap disappears. A physiotherapist can assess abdominal-wall function, symptoms, breathing and the movements you want to return to.

Seek help at any time for troubling symptoms. If a gap remains obvious around eight weeks after birth, discuss it with your clinician; you do not need to wait that long if you are uncomfortable. Recovery varies and some separation persists. The goal is comfortable function and a manageable activity plan, not proving that your abdomen has returned to a particular appearance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

General pregnancy exercise advice and individual plank suitability are different decisions.

Abdominal-exercise trials do not establish a universal plank prescription or a diastasis cure.

Postnatal progression depends on healing, symptoms and control, not a single gap measurement.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps connect questions about planks with practical adjustments, realistic expectations and the signs that need professional care.

When to seek help

This guide cannot clear a complicated pregnancy for exercise or diagnose diastasis. Stop for symptoms and seek immediate care for serious maternal warning signs. Use individual maternity and pelvic-health advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Planks are optional; choose the version and load that fit your pregnancy and symptoms.
  • A dome or gap is not, by itself, proof of injury or a test of exercise clearance.
  • Wall, incline or knee support can reduce difficulty, but do not guarantee suitability.
  • Keep breathing and seek help for pain, pressure, leaking or persistent difficulty controlling the movement.
  • Return after birth gradually, and treat maternal warning signs as medical concerns.

Frequently asked questions

Which plank or core exercises are unsuitable in pregnancy?

Avoid a version that causes pain, pressure, marked doming, loss of control or breath-holding. Medical complications can require additional limits. Avoid bump compression and prolonged flat-on-back exercise later in pregnancy; ask about specific movements rather than using a universal list.

What benefits can planks offer?

An appropriate version can contribute to trunk strength and control. It cannot guarantee prevention of leaking or diastasis, an easier birth or faster recovery. It is one optional part of a balanced routine.

What is an incline plank?

The upper body is supported higher than the floor, for example against a solid wall or suitable fixed counter. Less lean and higher support can reduce demand. Check stability, space for the bump, comfortable alignment and normal breathing.

Can I keep doing planks throughout pregnancy?

Some people continue adapted versions, while others prefer to stop. Symptoms, pregnancy complications and changing control matter more than a universal week or time target. Review the plan as your body changes.

Does doming mean I have damaged my muscles?

Not by itself. It is a cue to reassess the load and technique, especially if pronounced or accompanied by symptoms. Reduce the challenge and ask a pelvic-health professional if it persists.

Will drawing my tummy in prevent diastasis?

There is no guaranteed prevention exercise. Gentle coordinated activation differs from forcefully sucking in or holding your breath. Research on selected abdominal programmes does not justify a promise that bracing will keep the gap closed.

When can I restart after birth?

Start with recovery-appropriate gentle activity and progress according to healing, symptoms and professional advice. Complicated delivery or caesarean recovery can take longer. A routine check or calendar date is not automatic clearance for a full plank.

Must the gap close before I do any abdominal exercise?

No. Appropriate rehabilitation can include abdominal exercise while separation remains. The right load depends on function and symptoms, not finger width alone. Seek assessment for a persistent obvious gap or troubling pain, pressure or leaking.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
